wonder/tree.title: The Tree That Fell Down
wonder/tree.deck: A storm, a pine on the ground, and a question nobody had asked
wonder/tree.body:
One night there was a big storm.

The wind pushed and pushed on a tall pine tree at the edge of the woods. The
tree bent, and swayed, and creaked. And in the morning, when the sun came up,
the tree was lying down on the ground.

Its roots were sticking up in the air, still holding on to the dirt. Its top
was lost in the bushes. And in between was the trunk: long, and straight, and
round, like the biggest pencil you have ever seen.

Most people who walk past a fallen tree see a problem. *It's in the way. It
will rot. Somebody should cut it up for firewood.*

But the builder in this story looked at the tree and asked a different
question.

*What if this tree could become a house?*

That sounds silly at first. Houses are made of boards from the store, aren't
they? Flat, square boards, all the same.

But here is a secret about boards. Every board in the store started out as a
round tree, just like this one. Somebody cut the tree down. Somebody dragged it
out of the woods. A truck carried it to a mill. Big saws cut it into squares,
and a lot of the round tree was cut away and thrown on a pile. Then the boards
were dried, and smoothed, and sorted, and loaded on another truck, and carried
to a store, and stacked on a shelf, and sold.

That is a lot of hands, and a lot of trucks, and a lot of waiting, before a
single board reaches the house.

And this tree was already here. Right where the house could be.

So the builder made a plan: no mill, no truck, no store. Just the tree, a
small saw, a lot of careful thinking -- and a lot of help from the shape of
the tree itself.

The rest of this book is that plan.

:::box do "Try it together"
Go for a walk and look for a fallen tree or a big fallen branch. When you
find one:

1. Find where it is straight, and where it starts to bend or branch.
2. Wrap a piece of string around the fattest straight part, and mark the
   string with your finger. That is how fat the tree is *all the way round*.
3. Walk along it and count your steps from the fat end to where the straight
   part stops.

Take the string home. You will use it again on rung two.
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The method in this book builds a cabin frame from trees split on the spot with
one chainsaw. The reference dome is {{dome.diameter_ft}} feet across with
{{dome.floor_sqft}} square feet of floor, framed from {{dome.members}} wooden
members. What matters about a tree at this stage is only three things: how
fat it is at the bottom, how fat at the top of the straight part, and how long
that straight part is. Everything else in the plan is worked out from those.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
How many different people do you think touch a board before it gets to the
store?
:::

wonder/split.title: Cut It Like a Cake
wonder/split.deck: Half, half again, and half once more -- and every piece the same
wonder/split.body:
First, the builder cut the long trunk into shorter pieces, each one about as
long as a grown-up is tall. Each piece was a fat round log, like a giant spool
of thread.

Then came the clever part.

Have you ever cut a birthday cake? You cut it right down the middle, and you
have two halves. You cut each half down the middle, and you have four. You cut
each of those down the middle, and you have **eight** pieces.

And here is the magic: all eight pieces are the same shape. You did not have
to measure anything. You did not have to be careful about the angle. The cake
was round, so cutting it in half, and half again, and half again, gives eight
pieces that match -- because the cake did the measuring for you.

The builder did exactly that to each round log, with a chainsaw, carefully, in
long straight cuts down its length.

Half. Half again. Half again.

Eight sticks came out of every log. Each one was shaped like a long slice of
cake: pointy at the middle of the log, and round on the back where the bark
is. A stick shaped like that is called a **wedge**.

Most builders would never do this. They would cut the round log into square
boards. But try to cut a square out of a circle, and look at what is left: four
rounded corners of perfectly good wood, thrown away.

The cake cut throws almost nothing away. Every slice is used.

:::box do "Try it together"
You need two things that are round -- two oranges, two round slices of bread,
or a round cake (the best one, because you get to eat it after).

1. Cut the first one in half, then each half in half, then each quarter in
   half. Count the pieces. Are they the same?
2. Now try to cut the biggest *square* you can out of the second one. Put the
   leftover pieces in a pile.
3. Which way wasted less?
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The trunk is cut into sections, and each section is ripped lengthwise with a
chainsaw through its centre: once to halve it, twice to quarter it, four times
to make {{cut.splits}} sectors of {{cut.sector}} degrees each. No angle is ever
measured; the round log supplies the symmetry. Split this way, a trunk keeps
about {{pine.wedge_pct}} per cent of its wood as usable members; sawn into
two-by-fours, the same log keeps about {{pine.sawn_model_pct}} per cent. The cuts
are made with the saw -- never with a maul or a splitting wedge -- and only by
an adult in full safety gear.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
Why do all eight pieces come out the same, even though nobody measured them?
:::

wonder/triangle.title: The Shape That Will Not Wobble
wonder/triangle.deck: Push a square and it leans; push a triangle and it holds
wonder/triangle.body:
The wedges were not perfect. Some were a little bent. Some had a knot, or a
bump, or one side a little fatter than the other. A tree is not a factory.

A worried builder might say: *How can I build a house out of sticks that are
not perfect?*

The answer is a shape. The **triangle**.

Here is how to see it. Make a square out of four sticks, with a loose pin at
each corner. Now push the top corner sideways. What happens? The square leans
over. It squashes into a diamond, and then it falls flat. Nothing broke -- the
sticks are still the same length -- but the square could not hold its shape.

Now make a triangle out of three sticks, with a loose pin at each corner. Push
it. Push it harder.

It will not lean.

A triangle cannot change its shape unless one of its sticks gets longer or
shorter. And a stick does not want to get longer or shorter. So the triangle
holds.

That is why bridges, and swings, and roofs are full of triangles. And that is
why the builder's house is made of nothing *but* triangles. When every part of
a building is a triangle, the building holds its shape all by itself -- even if
the sticks are a little bent, or a little bumpy.

The builder liked to say it like this: *your head is not perfectly even on
both sides either, and it still protects your brain just fine.*

The sticks are allowed to be a little bit wrong. The triangles make them
strong.

:::box do "Try it together"
Cut seven strips of cardboard or stiff paper, all about the same length, and
make a hole near each end. Join four into a square and three into a triangle,
with paper fasteners (or a pencil poked through) at the corners.

Push each one sideways. Which one wobbles? Now add one more strip across the
square, corner to corner. What happened to the wobble?
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
A square frame is a mechanism: its corners turn and it racks over. A triangle
is fixed by the lengths of its three sides, so a frame made only of triangles
carries loads along its members -- push and pull, end to end -- rather than by
bending them. That is what lets a split log with a bow, a knot or an uneven
section be a structural member here. The two parts that do have to be right are
the skin, because water gets in, and the ground, because everything sits on
it. Later rungs return to both.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
How many triangles can you find holding something up, in your house or on your
street?
:::

wonder/dome.title: A Ball Made of Triangles
wonder/dome.deck: Twenty triangles make a ball, a few more make it round, and half of it is a house
wonder/dome.body:
If triangles are so strong, how do you make a whole house out of them?

Start with a ball.

Take twenty triangles, all exactly the same, and fit them together edge to
edge. They fold up into a shape like a big jewel, or a twenty-sided game die.
It is almost a ball -- but it is a bit too pointy. You could not live in a
jewel.

So the builder did something clever. Each big triangle was cut into four
smaller triangles, like cutting a sandwich into four. Then every new corner was
pushed out, just a little, until it touched the skin of a perfect ball.

Now the shape is much rounder. It is made of eighty small triangles, and it
looks like a ball made of glass panes.

And then the builder cut the ball in half -- right around its middle, like an
egg cup.

Half a ball sits flat on the ground. It has a floor. It has a roof that comes
all the way down to be its walls. That is a house: a **dome**.

This dome has {{dome.panels}} triangles. Count them in the picture if you
like. And here is the best part: there are only *two* kinds.

* {{dome.aaa}} of them have all three sides the same length.
* {{dome.bab}} of them have one long side and two sides that are a little
  shorter.

So in the whole house there are only two lengths of stick: a long one and a
slightly shorter one. If you can cut two lengths, you can build the whole thing.

:::box do "Try it together"
Find something in your house made of flat shapes put together into a round
one: a soccer ball, a lampshade, a wooden toy. Count the shapes. Are any of them
the same?

If you have a soccer ball, look for the five-sided patches. There are always
twelve of them, on every soccer ball in the world. Rung six tells you why.
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The shape is a two-frequency ("2V") geodesic hemisphere. It begins as an
icosahedron, the twenty-faced solid; every edge is halved, the midpoints are
pushed out onto the sphere, and the sphere is cut at its equator. The result
has {{dome.panels}} panels, {{dome.vertices}} corners and only two edge lengths,
in the ratio {{mb.ratio}} to one. The reference dome is {{dome.diameter_ft}}
feet across and {{dome.height_ft}} feet tall at the centre.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
Why did the builder cut the ball in half, instead of living inside a whole one?
:::

wonder/joint.title: Holding Hands Around the Corner
wonder/joint.deck: Three sticks, no knot in the middle, and a corner left empty on purpose
wonder/joint.body:
Now the builder had a pile of wedges in two lengths, and a plan for a ball of
triangles. But how do you hold three sticks together at a corner?

Many dome builders use a metal star at every corner. All the sticks run into
the star, and bolts hold them there. It works -- but only if every stick is
exactly the same, exactly straight and exactly the right length. Remember the
wedges? They are *not* exactly anything. A metal star would not fit them.

So the builder did something surprising. At the corners of these triangles,
**the sticks do not meet at all.**

Here is how. Hold three pencils in a triangle. Instead of making their ends
touch in the corners, slide each pencil along a little, so that the end of one
pencil rests on the *side* of the next one. The end of the first rests on the
side of the second. The end of the second rests on the side of the third. The
end of the third rests on the side of the first.

They go round and round, like children holding hands in a circle where each
one holds the next one's elbow. Or like the blades of a pinwheel. And right in
the corner, where you would expect the sticks to meet, there is... nothing.
Just air.

Because each stick only has to rest on a flat side, it does not need to be
perfect. A side is a big place to land.

And every triangle has its *own* three sticks. Where two triangles sit next to
each other, two sticks lie side by side, with a thin strip of wood called a
**key** pressed between them, like the filling in a sandwich.

:::box do "Try it together"
Take three craft sticks, pencils or straws. Lay them on the table in a
triangle so that the end of each one rests on the side of the next, going round
in the same direction. Now try going round the other way. Do you get the same
triangle, or its mirror image?
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
This is the pinwheel joint, and the frame is hubless: each member's butt end
lands on the flat sawn side of its neighbour, and no two ends ever meet. Every
panel owns all three of its members, which is why a dome of {{dome.panels}}
panels has {{dome.members}} members rather than one per edge, and why two
members and a key sit in each of the {{dome.seams}} seams. The butt end carries
the frame's one compound cut, made against a fixed setting; the other end is
left long and sawn off flush once the panel is together.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
Why would leaving the corner empty make the building easier to make?
:::

wonder/panel.title: Forty Triangles on a Table
wonder/panel.deck: Build every piece flat, on one table, the same way every time
wonder/panel.body:
Imagine trying to build a ball of triangles up in the air, on a wobbly ladder,
holding three long sticks at once and a drill in your teeth.

The builder did not want to do that. So the triangles were built somewhere
much nicer: flat on a table, on the ground.

The table was special. Before any wood went on it, the builder screwed little
blocks onto it in exactly the right places -- blocks to hold the first stick,
blocks to hold the second, blocks to hold the third, and a straight edge to
guide the saw. A table like that is called a **jig**.

With a jig, nobody needs to measure anything twice. You put the first stick
against its blocks. You put the second stick against its blocks. You put the
third stick against its blocks. You fasten them together. You saw the long
ends off along the guide. And off the table comes a triangle -- exactly like
the last one, and exactly like the next one.

Then you do it again. And again. Forty times.

Making the same thing over and over sounds boring. But it is the secret of how
one person can build a house. The first triangle takes a while, because you are
learning. By the fourth one, your hands know what to do. By the fortieth, you
could almost do it with your eyes closed (please don't).

And because each triangle is finished on the ground, it can be checked, and
fixed, and even painted, before it ever goes up.

:::box do "Try it together"
Draw one triangle on a piece of cardboard. Push a pin into the cardboard at
each corner, just outside the lines. Now lay a sheet of paper on the
cardboard, and trace a triangle using the pins as your guide -- then another
sheet, and another.

Lay all your paper triangles on top of each other. Are they the same? Now try
drawing three triangles *without* the pins and compare.
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The jig is one flat board that holds every member against fixed stops, so the
position of each stick -- not a tape measure -- decides the panel's shape.
The dome needs {{dome.aaa}} panels of one shape and {{dome.bab}} of the other,
so the jig is set up twice. Repeatability beats accuracy when you need forty
of something: a jig that is slightly off builds forty panels that still agree
with each other, and agreeing is what makes the dome close.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
What is something you have done so many times that your hands know how to do
it without you thinking?
:::

wonder/raise.title: Up, Up, Up
wonder/raise.deck: The bottom ring first, then the next, then the very top
wonder/raise.body:
Forty triangles were stacked up and ready. Now it was time to make them into a
house.

You cannot start at the top. The top has nothing to stand on. So the builder
started at the bottom.

First the bottom ring: the triangles that touch the ground, all the way round
in a circle. Then the next ring of triangles, leaning in, resting on the first.
Then the next. Every ring gets a little smaller, leaning in a little more,
like the rings of a beehive.

While the rings are leaning, they want to fall inward. So the builder held
them up with long sticks pushed against them from inside, called **props**.
A triangle goes up -- a prop goes under it. Another goes up -- another prop.

And then, at the very top, the last few triangles close the hole in the roof.

Here is the wonderful part. The moment the top is closed, every triangle is
holding up every other triangle. Push on one, and it pushes on its neighbours,
and they push on theirs, all the way round and all the way down. The dome holds
itself. One by one, the props come out, and nothing falls.

The builder of this book did something even more daring. Instead of building
on the ground, the builder strung strong ropes between big living trees, like a
giant spider web in the air, and lifted each triangle up into the web with a
winch -- a machine that winds a rope around a drum. The triangles were joined
together up in the air, and the whole dome hung between the trees, like a
lantern.

:::box do "Try it together"
Stand up some books in a ring on the floor, leaning a little inward. Do they
fall? Now lean a second ring on top of the first. What did you need to keep
them from falling? Those are your props.
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
A dome goes up course by course from the base ring, propped from inside until
the crown closes; once it closes the shell carries itself and the props come
out. The author's own method builds in the air instead: a web of wire rope
between living trees, a {{web.winch_lb}}-pound 12-volt winch, and each triangle
lifted flat in a harness and joined in place. Raising anything heavy is
grown-up work, and nobody -- ever -- stands under a load that is hanging.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
Why does a dome hold itself up once the very top is closed, but not before?
:::

wonder/skin.title: A Coat for the Rain
wonder/skin.deck: One coat that keeps the water out, and soft warm layers underneath
wonder/skin.body:
The dome was standing. But if you stood inside it, you could look up through
every triangle and see the sky. The wind blew straight through. And when it
rained -- splash.

A house needs a coat.

Water is sneaky. It runs downhill, it creeps into cracks, and if it gets inside
wood and stays there, it makes the wood soft and rotten. A house can be strong,
and straight, and beautiful, and still be ruined by a little water that got in
and never got out. So the builder thought about water more carefully than
anything else.

The answer was one coat that keeps out every drop of rain. Just one. Like a
raincoat, or a shower cap pulled down over the whole dome. Everything else
goes *under* the coat, where it stays dry.

And under the raincoat? Warm, soft layers -- like the quilts on a bed. The
builder's quilts can be sewn from old clothes, the ones too worn out to wear.
Each layer makes the house a bit warmer. When winter comes, add another
quilt. The next winter, add another. A house that gets warmer every winter,
like a person putting on one more hat.

There is one more sneaky kind of water: the kind that comes from inside. When
it is warm in the house and cold outside, your breath makes tiny drops on the
cold walls, just like on a cold window. So the builder left the house a way to
breathe, and a place for that water to drip out.

:::box do "Try it together"
Take two pieces of paper and a tray. On the first, lay three strips of paper
side by side with their edges just touching, and tape them. On the second, lay
three strips *overlapping* like roof shingles, the top one over the middle one
over the bottom one. Tilt each like a roof and sprinkle water from the top.
Which one lets water through to the tray?
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The skin, not the frame, is the part of a dome that has to be right, because
water is what ruins wooden buildings. This design uses exactly one watertight
layer -- a cap over the whole shell -- with insulation underneath it. The
insulation is quilted from recycled clothing: about {{tt_quilt.shirts_per_layer}}
t-shirts a layer, each layer adding R-{{tt_quilt.r_per_layer}}, added one winter
at a time. Moisture from inside is handled on purpose, by letting the shell
breathe and draining water at the rim.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
Where does the water on the inside of a cold window come from?
:::

wonder/ground.title: A Good Place to Stand
wonder/ground.deck: A house is only as steady as the ground under its ring
wonder/ground.body:
Have you ever sat at a table with one short leg? Every time you lean on it, it
wobbles. Clunk. Clunk.

A dome is a little like that table. All of its weight comes down through its
bottom ring: a circle of {{dome.base_sides}} corners sitting on the ground. If
the ground under one corner is lower than the others, or soft, or sinks when
it rains, the whole dome leans a little -- and a dome that leans a little at
the bottom leans more at the top.

So the builder said: *the frame is allowed to be a little bit wrong. The ground
is not.*

The ground under the ring has to be level, all the way round. And it has to be
strong enough not to sink. There are lots of ways to make good ground: a ring
of flat stones, a bed of packed gravel, a wooden deck on short posts, or a
concrete floor. The builder checks the ring by measuring straight across it,
corner to corner, in several directions. If every measurement is the same,
the ring is round. If one is different, the ring is telling you where it is
wrong, while it is still easy to fix.

And here is an idea that is bigger than one house. What if one family owned a
good flat piece of ground with water and electricity ready, and another family
brought their dome and set it down there? The ground stays; the dome can move
on someday. The builder calls that ground a **pad**.

:::box do "Try it together"
Make a ring of ten paper cups or toy blocks on a pillow, and set a plate on top.
Now do the same on a flat table. Push gently on each plate. Which one rocks?

Then measure across your table ring with a string in three different
directions. Are the three the same?
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The base ring is the one place in the method where error does not get absorbed
-- it accumulates, because every course above stands on whatever circle the
ring actually is. That is why the ring is checked across opposite corners when
it is set and again as the first courses go on. Footings range from gravel to
a slab; the options and their costs are on rung three. A pad is serviced ground
built once and shared or rented, so the dome on it can be moved.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
What is the steadiest thing you have ever stood on, and why was it steady?
:::

wonder/uses.title: What Will It Be?
wonder/uses.deck: The same round frame can be a bedroom, a workshop, a greenhouse or a sauna
wonder/uses.body:
Here is a riddle. What is round, made of triangles, and can be a bedroom, a
workshop, a greenhouse, a sauna, a garage, a studio, a gym and a cold room for
keeping food?

The answer: the same dome.

Every triangle in the dome is an opening. What you put *in* the opening decides
what the building is. Put windows in, and it is full of light. Put a door in,
and you can walk through. Put clear panels in the top, and plants can grow
inside. Put a little chimney through one, and you can have a wood stove. Put
in solid, warm panels, and it is a cosy bedroom.

So the builder thinks of the bare frame like a seed, or like a baby cell in
your body that has not decided yet whether it will be skin, or bone, or brain.
Scientists call a cell like that a **stem cell**. The frame is the stem cell.
The panels decide what it grows into.

And if you change your mind? Take a panel out and put a different one in. The
greenhouse can become a bedroom. The bedroom can become a workshop. The frame
does not mind. It stays exactly the same.

There is one more piece the builder treats as special: a column right in the
middle of the floor that carries water, power and drains. It is the most
expensive part, so it is built to unbolt and move with the family to the next
dome, the way you would take your favourite chair when you move house.

:::box do "Try it together"
Draw a big circle on a piece of paper. That is your dome's floor. Decide what
your dome is for, and draw what goes inside it. Then turn the paper over, draw
another circle, and make the same dome into something completely different.
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The "stem cell" is the project's name for the bare frame, skin, core and one
blank panel, with the building's purpose deferred to the panels hung in its
forty openings. The catalogue prices {{seed.count}} fit-outs on the same body,
from {{seed.cheapest_usd}} dollars for the bare article to {{seed.dearest_usd}}
dollars for the most fitted. Many of them are utility buildings -- storage, a
workshop, a greenhouse, a studio -- which is usually where a family's first
dome earns its keep.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
If you could have one round room all to yourself, what would it be for?
:::

wonder/count.title: Counting the Hours
wonder/count.deck: How long a house takes, and why counting honestly matters
wonder/count.body:
How long does it take to build a house?

For most houses, the answer is: a long time, a lot of people and a lot of money.
The builder of this book wanted to know exactly how long *this* house would
take, so they counted.

They counted the hours of cutting wedges at the log: about {{hr.split}} hours.
They counted cutting the ends of the sticks, and building the triangles on the
jig, and lifting them up into a dome. And then -- because the first time you
build anything, things go wrong -- they added extra hours just for mistakes.

All together the frame came to about {{clock.total}} hours. A grown-up's
working week is {{clock.week}} hours. So the frame of the house fits inside one
week of work. That is why this book is called *The 40 Hour Cabin*.

But the builder was careful to say what the forty hours do *not* include:
cutting down the trees, putting the coat on, the floor, the door, the windows.
Those come after, and they take longer. All of it together is about
{{money.labour_hours}} hours of building.

The builder was also careful about something else. Some of those numbers were
*measured* -- timed with a clock while the work was really done. Others were
*guesses*, good guesses, but guesses. In this book, every number says which kind
it is. Because a number that pretends to be measured when it was guessed is a
kind of fib, and you cannot build a house on fibs.

:::box do "Try it together"
Get a clock or a timer. Time how long it takes to cut out and tape together
{{mb.timed}} paper triangles. Now work out how long forty would take: forty is
{{mb.timed_times}} lots of {{mb.timed}}. Was your guess before you started close
to the real answer?
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
The forty-hour clock covers the frame, from wedges to standing:
{{clock.split_h}} hours of splitting at the measured rate of
{{hr.split_session}} wedges per {{hr.session}}-hour session, then cutting,
panels and raising as estimates, plus the owner's own error allowance of
{{clock.error_h}} hours. Felling, the skin, the floor and the openings are not
on that clock; the whole build is about {{money.labour_hours}} hours. Measured
and estimated figures are labelled as such everywhere in this book.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
Why does it matter whether a number was measured or guessed?
:::

wonder/care.title: Grown-Up Jobs and Helper Jobs
wonder/care.deck: The saw is a grown-up's job; the counting, sorting and painting are yours
wonder/care.body:
Building a house is a team job. And on every good team, everybody has the right
job.

Some jobs are grown-up jobs. The chainsaw is a grown-up job: it is sharp, and
fast, and very loud, and it does not care whose leg is in the way. Cutting
down a tree is a grown-up job too, and even grown-ups who have done it a
hundred times are careful every single time. Climbing ladders, lifting heavy
triangles, working with electricity and water pipes -- all grown-up jobs.

When a grown-up uses the chainsaw, they wear special clothes. A hard hat with a
screen over the face. Ear protectors, because the saw is loud enough to hurt
your ears. Thick gloves. Strong boots. And special trousers called **chaps**,
full of tough threads that can stop a chain if it ever touches them.

And there is one rule the builder never, ever breaks: **nobody uses the saw
alone.** There is always somebody else there -- standing well back, watching,
ready to help.

So what can a helper do? Lots!

A helper can count the sticks and sort them into piles by length. A helper
can mark each stick with a crayon so everybody knows which pile it belongs to.
A helper can hold the end of the measuring tape. A helper can draw the plans,
time the work and write down the numbers. A helper can build the paper models
that show everybody what the real house will look like. A helper can help oil
the wood -- with gloves on. And a helper can ask the best questions of all.

The most important job on any team is the one that keeps everybody safe.

:::box do "Try it together"
Make two lists on one piece of paper. On one side, write "Grown-up jobs". On
the other, "Helper jobs". Go through the twelve chapters of this rung and put
every job you can think of on one list or the other. Is there anything you are
not sure about? Ask!
:::

:::box why "For the grown-up"
Children stay well outside any felling zone -- at least two tree-lengths from a
tree being cut -- and away from a running saw. Chainsaw work needs a helmet with
a visor, hearing protection, gloves, boots and chainsaw chaps, and a second
person present every time. Oily rags from finishing can catch fire by
themselves: they go straight into a metal tin of water. Before anyone sleeps
in a building made this way, an engineer and the local building department
must have seen it. Rung three turns all of this into a written plan.
:::

:::box wonder "Wonder question"
What is the bravest thing a person can say on a building site? (Hint: it is
"wait".)
:::

understand/tree.title: Measure a Tree
understand/tree.deck: Three numbers -- the fat end, the thin end and the straight length -- and a string to find them
understand/tree.body:
A builder planning a house from a tree needs to know only three things about
the tree. Not its age, not its species, not what a timber buyer would pay for
it. Just these:

1. **How fat it is at the bottom** of the straight part (the *butt*).
2. **How fat it is at the top** of the straight part, where the first big
   branch starts.
3. **How long the straight part is**, from the butt to the first big branch or
   bend.

The fat bottom matters because a fatter log gives fatter sticks. The thin top
matters because the sticks from the top of the tree will be the thinnest ones
in the pile. And the length matters because the trunk is cut into pieces of
one length -- about as long as one person can carry -- and the number of pieces
decides how many sticks the tree can give.

The picture shows a worked example, the tree measured in Volume B: fat at the
bottom, thinner at the top, and long enough to cut into eight pieces of the
same length.

How do you measure how fat a tree is? You cannot put a ruler across the middle
of a trunk. But you can put a string *around* it, and a little bit of maths
does the rest.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** a long piece of string, a tape measure, a marker or chalk, a
notebook, and a calculator.

1. Find a fallen tree or log (or a standing tree, for practice). Find where
   the straight part starts and stops. Chalk a line at each end.
2. Wrap the string around the trunk at the bottom chalk line, pull it snug and
   pinch it where it meets itself. Measure the string to your pinch. Write it
   down: that is the distance *around*.
3. Do the same at the top chalk line.
4. Divide each distance around by **3.14**. The answers are the two
   *diameters* -- how fat the trunk is straight through.
5. Measure the straight part from chalk line to chalk line.
6. Now count: how many six-foot pieces fit in the straight part? (Throw away
   the leftover -- a short piece is firewood.) Each piece will give eight
   sticks. How many sticks does your tree give?
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
The distance around a circle is always about 3.14 times the distance across
it -- that number is called *pi*, and it is the same for every circle in the
world. So a string tells you the diameter without cutting anything. The
reference trunk in Volume A is {{cut.trunk}} inches across; a string around
it would measure {{mb.trunk_around_in}} inches. The cabin needs
{{dome.members}} sticks, and every six-foot section gives eight, so a planner
works out the number of trees from these three measurements alone -- that
sum is the first worksheet on rung three.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You have written down the bottom diameter, the top diameter and the straight
length of one real trunk, and you can say how many sticks it would give.
:::

understand/split.title: Eight From One
understand/split.deck: Halve something round three times, then try to cut squares out of it, and count what is left over
understand/split.body:
On rung one, a cake showed why cutting a round log in half three times gives
eight matching pieces. This chapter checks it two ways -- by folding, which
needs no knife at all, and by trying the alternative, which is to cut squares
out of a circle and see what is lost.

The real cut is made with a chainsaw, by an adult, along the whole length of a
six-foot log: once through the middle to make two halves, then each half
through the middle to make quarters, then each quarter to make eighths. The
picture shows the order. It is the order that matters, because after the first
cut every piece has a flat side to sit on, and a piece that sits still is a
piece a saw can cut safely.

Every cut runs through the very centre of the log -- the *pith*, the small dark
dot where the tree started growing. Because every cut goes through the centre,
every piece ends up with a point at the centre and a curved back of bark. The
log is round, so every piece is the same.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** three paper circles (trace round a plate), scissors, a ruler, and
a protractor if you have one.

1. **Fold it.** Fold the first circle exactly in half. Fold it in half again.
   And again. Unfold it. Count the triangle-shaped pieces between the creases.
   Use a protractor to measure the point of one piece.
2. **Cut it.** Cut the second circle along its creases into eight wedges.
   Stack them. Do they match?
3. **Try squares.** On the third circle, draw the biggest square you can fit
   inside it, with its corners touching the edge. Cut the square out. Now put
   the four leftover curved pieces next to your eight wedges from step two.
   Which pile of *useful* pieces is bigger?
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
Halving a circle three times divides it into {{cut.splits}} equal sectors of
{{cut.sector}} degrees, and nobody has to measure an angle: folding (or
sawing) through the middle is the measurement. A square inside a circle
wastes its four curved sides -- and a mill cutting rectangular boards out of a
round log wastes those sides too, plus the sawdust of many more cuts. Split
into wedges, a trunk keeps about {{pine.wedge_pct}} per cent of its wood;
sawn into two-by-fours, about {{pine.sawn_model_pct}} per cent. The real log is
cut lengthwise with a chainsaw, by an adult wearing full safety gear, with a
second person present -- never with an axe, a maul or a splitting wedge.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You can explain, without a picture, why three halvings give eight equal pieces
-- and why a square wastes wood that a wedge keeps.
:::

understand/triangle.title: The Wobble Test
understand/triangle.deck: Paper strips and paper fasteners prove the oldest rule in building
understand/triangle.body:
On rung one a triangle held and a square fell over. Here is the test done
properly, with one more experiment added at the end -- the one that shows how
far a triangle forgives a stick that is not straight.

The picture shows what you are about to see. Push the top of a rectangle
sideways and it *racks*: the corners turn and it leans over, even though
every stick stays the same length. A rectangle can only stand up if something
else holds its corners square -- a sheet nailed across it, or a stick running
corner to corner. That corner-to-corner stick turns the rectangle into two
triangles, and *that* is what holds it.

A triangle has nothing to turn. Its three corners are fixed by the lengths of
its three sides. For the triangle to change shape, a side would have to get
longer or shorter, and wood is very bad at changing length when you push or
pull it from the ends. That is the whole secret of a dome, and the reason a
dome needs no walls to brace it.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** eight strips of card about 15 cm long and 2 cm wide, a hole punch,
and paper fasteners (split pins).

1. Punch a hole near each end of every strip.
2. Join four strips into a square and three into a triangle, one fastener in
   each corner, loose enough to turn.
3. Lay both flat and push one corner sideways. Watch the square fold.
4. Add the eighth strip across the square, corner to corner. Push again.
5. **The forgiving test.** Make a second triangle, but bend one strip into a
   gentle curve before you fasten it. Push. Now make a third with one strip
   bent into a deep curve. Push that one.
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
A shape made of hinged sides holds only if its side lengths fix its angles.
Three sides do; four or more do not. Load on a triangulated frame therefore
runs *along* its members, as push and pull, which is the direction wood is
strongest. That is why a gently bowed stick still works in this frame -- the
triangle holds it in line -- and also why the forgiveness has a limit: a stick
bowed so far that it bends further when pushed lets the triangle squash. Volume
B grades every wedge for exactly that before it goes on the jig.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You can say why the square needed the extra strip and the triangle did not,
and which of your bent triangles a builder would reject.
:::

understand/dome.title: Build the Paper Dome
understand/dome.deck: Forty paper triangles in two shapes, cut from the template and taped into the dome itself
understand/dome.body:
This is the biggest project on this rung, and it is the dome itself: the same
{{dome.panels}} triangles as the real cabin, in the same two shapes, put
together in the same pattern, at one-{{mb.paper_scale}}th of the size. The
template is at the end of this chapter, on two pages.

Look at the picture first. The real dome's edges come in two lengths, coloured
two ways. The long edge and the short edge are in the ratio {{mb.ratio}} to
one -- close enough to look the same, different enough that a triangle built
with the wrong one will not fit.

There are two kinds of triangle:

* **{{mb.paper_equi}} equal-sided triangles**, every side long;
* **{{mb.paper_iso}} short-sided triangles**, with one long side and two
  shorter ones.

The short-sided triangles always come in groups of five, with their short
sides together and their points meeting at one corner, like the petals of a
flower. Each group of five is a **cap**. There are {{mb.paper_caps}} caps: one
on top, and five round it. The ten equal-sided triangles fill the gaps between
the caps.

When you cut out a cap you will find something interesting. Five triangle
points laid flat side by side do not quite go all the way round: they add up
to {{mb.paper_five_deg}} degrees, not the 360 degrees of a full turn. There is
a thin slice missing -- {{mb.paper_gap_deg}} degrees of it. When you close that
gap with tape, the cap stops lying flat and bulges up into a shallow point.
**That missing slice is what makes the dome curve.** Every round thing made of
flat pieces gets its roundness exactly that way.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** the two template pages (print them at **100 per cent / actual
size** -- the check bar must measure 50 mm), scissors, clear tape, and a ruler.
For a dome {{mb.paper_double_cm}} cm across instead of {{mb.paper_diameter_cm}}
cm, enlarge both pages to 200 per cent.

1. Cut out the six caps along their solid outlines. Crease the dashed lines.
2. Close each cap: bring the two edges of its gap together and tape them. Each
   cap now bulges up like a very flat tent.
3. Cut out the ten equal-sided triangles.
4. Put one cap on the table, point up. That is the top. Tape an equal-sided
   triangle to each of its five bottom edges.
5. Between each pair of those triangles is a gap. Fit a cap into each gap,
   point up, and tape its two upper edges to the triangles on either side.
6. Between each pair of those five caps is one last gap at the bottom. Fit an
   equal-sided triangle into each, point up, one side along the table, and tape
   it to the caps beside it.
7. Stand it up. The bottom edge is a ring of ten long sides. Press gently on
   the top.
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
The dome is a two-frequency geodesic hemisphere: an icosahedron with each edge
halved and the new corners pushed out onto a sphere, then cut at the equator.
Its {{mb.corners}} corners are of three kinds -- {{mb.five_way}} where five
triangles meet (the tops of your caps), {{mb.six_way}} inside corners where six
meet, and {{mb.rim_corners}} round the bottom ring -- and its {{mb.edges}} edges
of two lengths: {{mb.long_edges}} long and {{mb.short_edges}} short. The real
cabin is the same object {{dome.diameter_ft}} feet across. Notice one more
thing: your paper triangles each have their own three edges, and the tape
between them is a seam. The real dome is built exactly that way, which is the
subject of the next chapter.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
Your paper dome stands by itself, and you can point to a five-way corner, a
six-way corner and the ten-sided ring at the bottom.
:::

[[template:paper-dome]]

understand/joint.title: Craft-Stick Pinwheels
understand/joint.deck: Three sticks, each end resting on the next one's side, and the corner left empty
understand/joint.body:
Most domes are held together at their corners by a *hub*: a metal star with a
socket for every stick. A hub only works when every stick arrives at exactly
the same angle and is exactly the right length. A pile of split logs never
does.

So the wedge dome has no hubs. At each corner of a triangle, the end of one
stick rests on the *side* of the next, and that one's end rests on the side of
the next, round and round like a pinwheel. The corner itself is empty. The
picture is a corner of the real frame, where five triangles meet and nothing
touches anything at the point.

This chapter builds both kinds of corner, and then does the test that shows why
the pinwheel wins with rough wood.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** about ten craft sticks, white glue (a grown-up can use a glue gun
instead), a few balls of modelling clay, and a pencil.

1. **The pinwheel.** Lay three sticks on the table in a triangle so that the end
   of each one rests on the side of the next, all going round the same way.
   Glue the three overlaps. That is one panel.
2. **The mirror.** Make a second pinwheel going round the *other* way. Lay it on
   the first. Do they match? (Builders pick one direction and use it for every
   panel, or the seams do not line up.)
3. **The seam.** Lay two pinwheel panels edge to edge, with a thin strip of
   card standing between the two sticks that touch. That strip is the *key*,
   and the pair of sticks with the key between them is a *seam*.
4. **The hub.** Push the ends of three sticks into one ball of clay so they
   meet at a point, making a triangle with a clay ball at each corner.
5. **The test.** Snap a little off the end of one stick in each triangle so it
   is shorter than the others. Try to rebuild both. Which one still closes?
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
In the pinwheel, a stick that is a little short simply slides along the side of
its neighbour and lands a little further in, and the panel still closes. The
error goes into the overlap instead of into the corner. On the real frame each
member's resting end -- the *butt* -- gets one careful compound cut. The other
end -- the *head* -- is left deliberately long and sawn off flush once the
panel is assembled, so the length is decided by the panel, not by a tape
measure. Because every panel has its own three members, the dome has
{{dome.members}} members for {{mb.edges}} edges, and each of its {{dome.seams}}
seams is two members with a key between them.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You have built two pinwheel panels and a seam, and you can say why the
pinwheel closed with a short stick when the hub did not.
:::

understand/panel.title: A Jig From a Box
understand/panel.deck: Pins in cardboard make every triangle the same, and a ruler cannot
understand/panel.body:
The real panels are built on a **jig**: one flat board with blocks screwed to
it that hold each stick in its place, and a straight edge the saw runs along.
The picture shows one, labelled. Once the blocks are set, nobody measures
anything again -- the blocks do the measuring, the same way every time.

Why go to the trouble? Because forty triangles that are each *almost* right
will not close into a dome. Every small difference adds up as the rings go on,
and the last triangle will not fit the hole that is left for it. Forty
triangles that are *the same* -- even if they are all the same slightly-wrong
size -- close perfectly, because they all agree with each other.

That is the most surprising idea in building: **making things the same matters
more than making each one perfect.**

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** the side of a cardboard box, a dozen pushpins, a ruler, a pencil,
and paper strips or straws cut to the paper dome's two lengths:
{{mb.paper_long_mm}} mm and {{mb.paper_short_mm}} mm.

1. **Freehand first.** Without the jig, build five short-sided triangles from
   your strips, using the ruler to place them. Tape each one.
2. **Make the jig.** Draw one short-sided triangle carefully on the cardboard.
   Push two pins just outside each corner, so a strip laid along a side is held
   by the pins.
3. **Jig run.** Build five more triangles by laying strips against the pins,
   taping, and lifting each finished triangle off.
4. **Compare.** Measure all three sides of all ten triangles. Write them in a
   table. Which group of five is more alike?
5. **The second shape.** The equal-sided triangles need their own jig. Make it.
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
A jig turns a measurement made once into a position held forever. The real jig
holds each wedge by its two flat sawn faces, never by its bumpy bark, and it
goes through twelve stages for every panel, from the bare bench to the finished
triangle lifted off. The dome needs {{dome.aaa}} equal-sided panels and
{{dome.bab}} short-sided ones, so the real jig is set up twice, just like yours.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
Your measurements show the jig triangles agreeing with each other better than
the freehand ones, and you can say why agreeing matters more than being exact.
:::

understand/raise.title: Raise It Ring by Ring
understand/raise.deck: The straw dome goes up from the bottom, one ring at a time, with props
understand/raise.body:
The paper dome was taped together in your hands. A real dome is far too heavy
for that: it goes up from the ground, ring by ring, and leans on props until the
top is closed. The straw dome is how you feel that happen.

The straw dome is built the *other* way from the real one. In a straw dome,
each straw is one edge, shared by the two triangles on either side of it -- so
it needs only {{mb.edges}} straws, where the real frame needs {{dome.members}}
members. That is how most domes in the world are built, with hubs. Build it, and
you will understand both the hub dome and the reason the wedge dome does not do
it that way.

The picture shows the real frame's first ring standing on its own, before
anything is above it.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** {{mb.straw_long_count}} straws cut to {{mb.straw_long_cm}} cm (the
long ones) and {{mb.straw_short_count}} cut to {{mb.straw_short_cm}} cm (trim
{{mb.straw_trim_cm}} cm off a long one), pipe cleaners cut into short pieces, a
few pencils for props, and your paper dome as a map.

1. **Joints.** Every corner is a little bundle of pipe-cleaner pieces twisted
   together, one piece poked into the end of each straw that meets there.
   There are {{mb.corners}} corners.
2. **The bottom ring.** Join ten long straws into a ring on the table.
3. **Ring by ring.** Copy your paper dome: every long edge is a long straw,
   every short edge a short one. Build upward from the ring one row of
   triangles at a time, going all the way round before you start the next row.
4. **Props.** When a row leans in and wants to fall, hold it up from inside with
   a pencil standing on the table. Count your props.
5. **Close the top.** The last five short straws meet at the top corner.
6. **Take the props out**, one at a time. Push gently on the dome.
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
A dome only carries itself once it is closed: until then each ring leans on the
one below and the leaning has to be held. Once the top closes, every triangle
pushes on its neighbours all the way round and down, and the props can come
out. The real frame goes up the same way, in courses -- the first course of
{{ring.first}} panels, the second of {{ring.second}}, then the {{ring.cap}}
round the top -- or, in the author's own method, is joined in the air on a web
of rope between living trees. Your straw dome is {{mb.straw_diameter_cm}} cm
across and {{mb.straw_height_cm}} cm tall.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
Your straw dome stands with every prop removed, and you can say why it needed
props before the top was closed and none after.
:::

understand/skin.title: The Raincoat Test
understand/skin.deck: A spray bottle shows why roofs overlap instead of trying to seal
understand/skin.body:
The frame is the part you are allowed to get wrong. The skin is not. A dome has
{{dome.seams}} seams, and every one is a place water could get in, and wood
that stays wet rots. So the skin is planned more carefully than anything else,
around two ideas you can test on the table.

**Shed, don't seal.** A seal tries to stop water by being perfect, and nothing
outdoors stays perfect: wood shrinks and swells, tape lifts, and the first gap
lets water in. A roof that *sheds* does not try to stop water at all. It hands
the water downhill, each layer overlapping the one below it, so the water is
always on top and always moving away.

**Water from the inside.** Warm air holds more water than cold air. When warm,
damp air from inside a house touches something cold, it drops some of its water
on it -- the way a cold glass gets wet on a summer day. That is *condensation*,
and it is why the inside of a dome has to be planned too, not just the outside.

The picture shows the dome dressed for winter: soft layers inside, one
watertight cap over them all.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** card or paper, wax paper, tape, a spray bottle of water, a tray, a
glass jar, ice and water.

1. **Seal or shed.** Make two little roofs from four strips of card each. On the
   first, butt the strips edge to edge and tape the joins. On the second, lay
   them overlapping like shingles, each strip over the one below. Tilt both on
   the tray and spray from above. Look underneath.
2. **One raincoat.** Cover your paper dome with a single piece of wax paper,
   pleated round it like a shower cap. Spray it. Is the paper under it dry?
3. **Water from nowhere.** Fill the jar with ice and water and leave it on the
   counter for ten minutes. Where did the water on the outside come from?
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
The cabin's design has exactly one watertight layer, the cap, with everything
else under it where it stays dry. Under the cap go quilted layers sewn from
recycled clothing, each adding R-{{tt_quilt.r_per_layer}} of warmth, added one
winter at a time. The water on your jar came out of the air: the jar was colder
than the air's *dew point*, the temperature at which it has to let water go.
Volume A spends a whole part on keeping the dome's seams above the dew point, or
deliberately catching the water where it is welcome.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You can say which roof kept the tray dry and why, and where the water on the jar
came from.
:::

understand/ground.title: The Wobbly Table Test
understand/ground.deck: A dome on a bumpy floor, and the measurement that finds it
understand/ground.body:
A dome stands on its bottom ring: {{mb.rim_edges}} edges and {{mb.rim_corners}}
corners touching the ground in a circle, as the picture shows from above. All
the weight of the building comes down through those ten corners.

That ring is the one place where a small mistake grows instead of
disappearing. A frame absorbs a short stick or a crooked one, because the
triangles share the error between them. But if the ring is not level, or not
round, every ring above it is built on a tilted or squashed circle, and the
error is carried all the way to the top. A corner a little low at the bottom
means a top a lot off at the apex.

The good news is that the ring is easy to check, with nothing but a string.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** your paper or straw dome, a flat board or tray, a coin, a ruler and
a piece of string.

1. **Level.** Stand the dome on the flat board. Measure from the board to the
   top point with the ruler.
2. **Low corner.** Slide a coin under one bottom corner. Measure the top again.
   How far did the top move compared with the thickness of the coin?
3. **Round.** Take the coin out. Stretch the string across the ring from one
   bottom corner to the corner exactly opposite, and mark it. Do the same for
   the other four opposite pairs. Are all five the same?
4. **Squash it.** Press the ring gently so it becomes a little oval, and measure
   the five pairs again. Which numbers changed?
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
A circle has the same width in every direction, so five equal measurements
across a ten-sided ring prove it is round, and one odd measurement points
straight at the corner that is wrong. The real builder makes this check when
the ring is first set, again after the first course, and again before the top
closes -- because the ring is the one error the frame cannot forgive. On real
ground, the ring stands on gravel, a deck, piers or a slab, and it is strapped
down: wind blowing over a dome tries to lift it, like a wing.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You can find a low or squashed corner on your dome using only the string, and
say why the ring is checked three times on the real build.
:::

understand/uses.title: Draw Your Round Room
understand/uses.deck: Rings of headroom on a paper floor, and where the bed goes
understand/uses.body:
A round room is not a square room with curved walls. It changes where you can
stand, where the furniture goes, and what the room is good for. Before anybody
builds a dome, it is worth drawing one -- because the answers are measurable,
and they surprise people.

The biggest surprise is headroom. The roof of a dome comes all the way down to
the floor at the edge. In the middle you can stand up easily; near the wall you
cannot. Of the reference dome's {{mb.floor_circle_sqft}} square feet of floor
circle, only {{mb.stand_sqft}} -- about {{mb.stand_pct}} per cent -- has
{{mb.head_ft}} feet or more of ceiling over it. The rest is a low ring round the
wall.

That low ring is not wasted. It is exactly the right height for the things that
do not need you to stand: beds, benches, low shelves, a desk with a window. A
well-planned round room puts the low things in the ring and keeps the tall,
open middle for walking, cooking and the table. The picture shows a dome
furnished that way.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** a big sheet of paper, a pencil tied to a piece of string, a ruler,
coloured pencils, and card for furniture.

1. **The floor.** At one centimetre to the foot, draw a circle {{mb.plan_cm}} cm
   across. That is the reference dome's floor.
2. **Standing room.** From the same centre, draw a second circle
   {{mb.plan_stand_cm}} cm across. Inside it, a grown-up can stand up straight.
   Shade the ring between the two circles.
3. **Furniture.** Cut out a bed, a table, a stove, a desk and some shelves from
   card, to the same scale (a bed is about 3 by 6.5 feet: 3 by 6.5 cm).
4. **Place them.** Low things in the shaded ring, tall things and walking space
   in the middle.
5. **Choose a purpose.** Make a second plan for a completely different use -- a
   workshop, a greenhouse, a studio.
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
A hemisphere's ceiling height drops from its full height at the centre to
nothing at the wall, so a fixed headroom draws a smaller circle inside the
floor. Two fixes exist and both are priced in the volumes: a short straight
wall under the rim lifts the whole dome and pushes the standing circle outward
(a *pony wall*), and furnishing the ring with low built-ins turns it from dead
floor into storage. Because the frame does not care what the room is for, the
same plan can be redrawn for any use.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
You have two plans for the same dome with different uses, and the bed is in the
ring in both.
:::

understand/count.title: Time It and Count It
understand/count.deck: Make five paper triangles against a clock, then work out forty
understand/count.body:
On rung one the builder counted the hours. This chapter counts the way a builder
counts -- by measuring a little and working out a lot -- and then looks at the
most important question to ask about any number: *was it measured, or guessed?*

Here is the real forty-hour clock from Volume A. Read the last column: it says
how each number was found.

    {{clock.table}}

Splitting is **measured**: the owner timed real sessions at the log. Cutting,
building panels and raising are **estimates**: careful, reasoned, but not yet
timed on a real build. The last line is the owner's own **allowance** for the
mistakes every first build makes. A book that hid the difference would look
more certain and be less true.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** a timer, paper, scissors, tape, a notebook, and your paper-dome
jig from chapter six.

1. **Measure.** Time yourself making {{mb.timed}} triangles on the jig. Write
   down the time for *each* triangle separately.
2. **Work it out.** The dome needs forty. Forty is {{mb.timed_times}} lots
   of {{mb.timed}}. Multiply your total. Write it down and label it *estimate*.
3. **Learning curve.** Look at your five separate times. Was the first one the
   slowest? Draw a little bar chart of the five.
4. **Measure again.** Now actually make the next five, and time them. Was your
   estimate high or low?
5. **Label everything.** Go back through your notebook and write *measured* or
   *estimated* next to every number.
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
Most of a build's time is repetition, and repetition gets faster: the first
panel off a jig is a rehearsal and the fourth is usually the first good one. An
estimate made from the first few is therefore usually high -- unless it forgets
the learning time, the tired afternoon or the rain day, which is what the
allowance is for. The forty hours cover the frame; the whole build, with the
skin, floor and openings, is about {{money.labour_hours}} hours, and the books
keep both numbers in view.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
Every number in your notebook is labelled measured or estimated, and you can
say which kind the real clock's splitting time is.
:::

understand/care.title: The Job Sorting Game
understand/care.deck: Cards, gear and the one rule that has no exceptions
understand/care.body:
On rung one, jobs were sorted into grown-up jobs and helper jobs. This chapter
turns that into a game a family can play before any real work starts -- and
ends with the one rule on a building site that has no exceptions.

Real builders do this. Before a crew starts a job, they talk through who does
what, what can go wrong, and what everybody does if it does. It is called a
*safety briefing*, and the best ones are short, clear and taken seriously by
everybody, including the youngest person on site.

:::box do "Make it"
**You need:** twenty index cards and a pen.

1. **Write the jobs.** One job per card: felling a tree, cutting a log to
   length, ripping wedges with the saw, carrying a wedge, sorting wedges by
   length, marking wedges with crayon, setting up the jig, screwing a panel,
   sawing the long ends off, oiling wood, lifting a panel, climbing a ladder,
   holding the tape, checking the ring with a string, wiring a light, timing
   the work, drawing the plan, building a model, making lunch, taking photos.
2. **Sort them** into three piles: *trained grown-up only*, *grown-up with a
   helper*, *helper*.
3. **Gear check.** For every card in the first pile, write on the back what the
   person must wear. (Chainsaw work: helmet with a face screen, ear protection,
   gloves, sturdy boots and chainsaw chaps.)
4. **The stop word.** Choose one word that anybody -- anybody at all -- can
   shout to stop all work instantly. Practise it. Everybody freezes, saws go
   off, nobody moves until the person who called it says why.
5. **The rule with no exceptions.** Write it on its own card: *Nobody uses the
   saw alone.*
:::

:::box why "Why it works"
Most accidents happen in the gap between what one person assumed and another
person did. Sorting the jobs out loud closes that gap before the work starts.
The stop word gives the smallest person on site the biggest power: to stop
everything when something looks wrong. On the real build, children stay at
least two tree-lengths away from any tree being felled and well clear of a
running saw, and the volumes add the rules for felling, ladders, lifting and
the trades that only licensed people do.
:::

:::box done "You've got it when"
Everybody in the family can say the stop word, the rule with no exceptions, and
which pile their own jobs are in.
:::

plan/tree.title: Your Trees, Measured
plan/tree.deck: From three numbers on a real trunk to the struts it gives and the dome it can make
plan/tree.body:
**What you are deciding:** whether the trees you have can make a frame, and how
many of them it takes.

## The reference answer

Volume B works its plan from one measured tree: {{tt_tree.butt_diameter_in}}
inches across at the butt, {{tt_tree.top_diameter_in}} inches at the top of the
straight part, and {{tt_tree.usable_length_ft}} feet of usable trunk between.

From those three numbers, everything follows:

* the trunk is cut into sections of {{tt_tree.section_length_ft}} feet -- the
  longest piece one person can carry and set alone -- which makes
  {{tt_tree.sections}} sections;
* each section is ripped into {{cut.splits}} wedges, so one tree gives
  {{tt_tree.struts_per_tree}} struts;
* the frame needs {{dome.members}} members, so it consumes
  {{tt_dome.trees_strictly_needed}} trees -- and the plan fells
  {{tt_dome.trees}}, because a pile always has rejects: a wedge with a crack
  down its point, a knot at its bearing end, a bow too deep to straighten.

The same tree holds {{tt_tree.solid_bf}} board feet of solid wood; split, it
keeps {{tt_tree.wedge_bf}} of them as members -- {{tt_tree.recovery_pct}} per
cent -- and loses {{tt_tree.kerf_bf}} board feet to the saw's cut.

## Thin trees and bent trees

A tree is not ruled out by being bent. A bend costs you the section it falls in,
not the tree: cut either side of it, burn the kink, and keep going. That is the
great advantage of short pieces.

A tree *is* ruled out by being too thin. The wedge has to carry as much wood as
the board it replaces. Volume B's strut has {{tt_log.member_area}} square inches
of section against a dressed two-by-four's {{tt_board.dressed_in2}}; a much
thinner tree would make sticks that lose that comparison, and then the honest
answer is to buy boards.

:::box do "Worksheet 1: my trees"
| | Tree 1 | Tree 2 | Tree 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Butt diameter (in) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Top diameter (in) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Straight length (ft) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Sections (length ÷ section, rounded down) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Struts (sections × {{cut.splits}}) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |

**Struts I have, all trees together:** [[blank]] · **Struts the frame needs, with
spares:** [[blank]] · **Measured by:** [[blank]] **on:** [[blank]]
:::

:::box why "Why"
The diameter at the middle of the trunk sets how wide the sticks are, and stick
width is the one thing that changes the cut list for a given dome (chapter five).
The length sets how many sections, and the section length sets the dome's size
(chapter four). Nothing else about the tree enters the arithmetic -- which is why
the method can use storm-fallen and low-grade trees a mill would never pay for.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Measure only the straight run: the flared butt and the crown above the first big
branch are firewood. Use the middle diameter, not the butt, when you size sticks;
the butt flatters you. And plan spares -- a pile with no rejects allowed is a
plan that assumes every stick is perfect, and no pile is.
:::

plan/split.title: The Splitting Plan
plan/split.deck: Sections, sectors, sessions and fuel: the part of the work that is measured, not guessed
plan/split.body:
**What you are deciding:** how many days at the log, how much fuel, and how the
saw work will be staffed.

## The reference answer

This is the one part of the build that is **measured**. The owner timed real
sessions at the log: {{hr.split_session}} wedges in a {{hr.session}}-hour
session. The reference frame is split from {{parts.sections}} log sections into
{{dome.members}} wedges, so the splitting takes {{hr.split}} hours.

The saw drank {{rip.tanks_hour}} tanks of fuel an hour while ripping (also
measured), which is {{rip.tanks}} tanks for all of it -- about {{rip.gal_lo}}
to {{rip.gal_hi}} US gallons. The calendar the paperback teaches gives the saw
{{rip.days}} days in all: {{rip.days_felling}} of felling,
{{rip.days_bucking}} of bucking the trunks to length and {{rip.days_ripping}} of
ripping.

Why split instead of saw into boards? The picture shows the same log converted
both ways. Packed with rectangles, a round log loses its curved sides; split
into eighths, it loses only the thin lines of the saw's cut. Volume B's tree
keeps {{tt_tree.recovery_pct}} per cent of its wood split, against about
{{tt_tree.sawn_recovery_pct}} per cent sawn into two-by-fours.

## How the cutting goes

Each section is cut lengthwise three times over: once through the centre to
halve it, then each half, then each quarter -- seven straight cuts, all through
the pith. The first cut is the only one where the log can roll, so the log sits
in a cradle; after that, every piece has a flat face to sit on. The wedges go
straight onto spacer sticks, bark up, to dry.

:::box do "Worksheet 2: my splitting plan"
| | Mine | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Sections to rip | [[blank]] | {{parts.sections}} |
| Wedges (sections × {{cut.splits}}) | [[blank]] | {{dome.members}} |
| My rate, wedges per session (measure it!) | [[blank]] | {{hr.split_session}} |
| Sessions (wedges ÷ rate) | [[blank]] | -- |
| Hours at the log | [[blank]] | {{hr.split}} |
| Tanks of fuel (hours × tanks per hour) | [[blank]] | {{rip.tanks}} |

**The second person at the log, every session:** [[blank]]
:::

:::box why "Why"
Halving needs no measured angle, so the saw does the geometry. A chain filed for
ripping cuts along the grain far faster than a crosscut chain, and a sharp chain
keeps the cut narrow -- a dull one widens it and eats the recovery. Splitting is
the largest single block of the frame's hours, which is why it is the one the
owner measured first.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Never alone at the log. Keep bar oil full: ripping buries the bar for minutes at
a time. File the chain at every fuel stop whether it asks or not. Aim every cut
through the pith -- a wedge whose point misses the centre has a soft, split-prone
edge exactly where it bears. And the split is a saw cut, always: this method does
not use axes, mauls or splitting wedges.
:::

plan/triangle.title: What Must Be Right, and What May Be Rough
plan/triangle.deck: The frame forgives; the skin and the ground do not -- so plan the care where it counts
plan/triangle.body:
**What you are deciding:** where to spend your care, your money and your
checking -- because they are not equally needed everywhere.

## The reference answer

The project's whole argument fits in one sentence from Volume A: *the frame is
the part you are allowed to get wrong; the skin and the ground are not.*

The frame forgives because it is made of triangles. Loads run along the members,
so a bowed or knotty stick still does its job, and the method gives every small
error somewhere harmless to go:

* a stick a little long or short -- the head is cut long and sawn off flush once
  the panel is together, so the panel decides the length;
* a butt end cut a degree off -- the screws pull it onto its neighbour's flat
  face;
* a seam a little wide or narrow -- the key and gasket take it up, shared across
  {{dome.seams}} seams.

Two places do not forgive.

**The skin**, because water that gets in stays in and rots the frame, however
good the frame is. That is chapter eight.

**The ground ring**, because its error does not get absorbed -- it grows. A
strut error of {{geo.ring_err}} inches in the base ring moves the ring's
diameter by {{geo.ring_d_err}} inches: the ring multiplies it
by {{geo.ring_gain}}. That is chapter nine.

:::box do "Worksheet 3: where my care goes"
| | What I will check | How | When | Who |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The ring is round and level | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Every wedge is graded | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| One watertight layer, unbroken | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| The inside can breathe and drain | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| The frame is strapped down | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
A triangulated shell resolves its loads axially, so asymmetry in it is absorbed
rather than amplified -- the lumpy frame in the picture stood. What it cannot do
is keep water out or correct the circle it stands on. Spending precision where
it pays and tolerance where the tree varies is the method's whole economy.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
"May be rough" does not mean "may be rotten". Volume B grades every wedge in four
passes before it reaches the jig: the bend, the knot in the middle third, the knot
at the bearing end, and a crack down the pith. A wedge that fails goes to
blocking, not to the frame.
:::

plan/dome.title: Choose Your Size
plan/dome.deck: One number decides the building, and the two books chose it two different ways
plan/dome.body:
**What you are deciding:** the dome's size -- one number, from which everything
else follows.

## The reference answers, and why there are two

Both books build a two-frequency hemisphere with {{dome.panels}} panels and
{{dome.members}} members. Both start from six feet, the longest stick one person
can carry and set alone. And they arrive at different sizes, because they apply
the six feet to different things.

**Volume A** takes six feet as the **long chord** -- the edge of the triangle,
corner to corner -- because that is what the owner's real members measure:
{{cut.a_chord}} inches long, {{cut.b_chord}} inches short. That gives a sphere of
radius {{dome.radius_in}} inches: a dome {{dome.diameter_ft}} feet across and
{{dome.height_ft}} feet tall, with {{dome.floor_sqft}} square feet of floor
inside its ten-sided ring.

**Volume B** takes six feet as the **longest piece you cut** -- the member
itself. Because of the pinwheel, a member is always a little shorter than the
edge it spans, so a six-foot member spans a longer edge, and the dome comes out
bigger: {{tt_dome.diameter_ft}} feet across, {{tt_dome.height_ft}} feet tall,
{{tt_dome.floor_sqft}} square feet counted as a full circle.

Neither is wrong. They are two honest ways of saying "six feet". Pick one
convention for your plan and never mix them.

## Standing room

Floor is not the same as room. Of Volume A's {{mb.floor_circle_sqft}} square
feet of floor circle, {{mb.stand_sqft}} -- about {{mb.stand_pct}} per cent --
has {{mb.head_ft}} feet or more over it; the rest is the low ring round the
wall, which is where beds, benches and storage belong.

## Bigger and smaller

The parts list does not change with size: a {{flat.small_ft}}-foot dome and a
{{flat.big_ft}}-foot dome both have {{dome.members}} members and
{{dome.panels}} panels, and the bigger one has {{flat.ratio}} times the floor.
What grows is the length of each stick, and the stick is limited by what one
person can lift. Past that, a bigger dome needs either a crew or a higher
frequency -- more, shorter sticks.

:::box do "Worksheet 4: my size"
| | Mine | Volume A | Volume B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Longest stick I can carry and set | [[blank]] | {{cut.a_chord}} in, as the chord | {{tt_dome.longest_member_in}} in, as the cut |
| Is that the chord or the cut member? | [[blank]] | chord | member |
| Long chord (in) | [[blank]] | {{cut.a_chord}} | -- |
| Sphere radius (long chord ÷ {{cut.a_factor}}) | [[blank]] | {{dome.radius_in}} in | {{tt_dome.radius_in}} in |
| Across (radius × 2 ÷ 12, ft) | [[blank]] | {{dome.diameter_ft}} | {{tt_dome.diameter_ft}} |
| Height at the centre (ft) | [[blank]] | {{dome.height_ft}} | {{tt_dome.height_ft}} |
:::

:::box why "Why"
Every edge of the dome is a fixed fraction of the sphere's radius -- the long one
{{cut.a_factor}}, the short one {{cut.b_factor}} -- so one length fixes them all.
The pinwheel then takes a bite off each member that depends on the stick's
width, not on the dome's size; that bite is why "six feet" means two different
domes. The volumes print both calculations and close the loop between them.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Decide the convention first and write it at the top of your plan. Check your size
against the stick you can actually lift, green and wet. And remember the
headroom: a hemisphere's usable floor is much smaller than its floor area.
:::

plan/joint.title: Your Cut List
plan/joint.deck: Two chords, two cut lengths, three saw settings and two keys
plan/joint.body:
**What you are deciding:** the cut list -- every length, every angle, every key --
before a single member is cut.

## The reference answer

Volume A's frame, solved by the project's simulator:

* **Two chords.** The long edge is {{cut.a_chord}} inches, the short
  {{cut.b_chord}} inches.
* **Two cut lengths.** A member stops short of the corner so its end can land on
  its neighbour's side. That *bite* depends on the stick's width
  ({{cut.width}} inches across the bark face, {{cut.depth}} inches deep from point
  to bark): {{cut.a_bite}} inches off a long member and {{cut.b_bite}} inches off
  a short one. So the long members are cut to {{cut.a_cut}} inches and the short
  ones to {{cut.b_cut}} inches -- {{parts.long_members}} of each length.
* **One compound cut.** The butt end of every member is cut once, to land flat on
  its neighbour: a bevel of {{cut.bevel}} degrees and one of only {{cut.mitres}}
  mitre settings for all {{dome.members}} members. The other end is left long and
  sawn flush on the jig.
* **Two keys.** The dome's {{dome.seams}} seams fold at only two angles:
  {{seam.fold_a}} degrees ({{tt_seam.count_a}} seams) and {{seam.fold_b}} degrees
  ({{tt_seam.count_b}} seams). Each takes its own key, {{seam.key_a}} and
  {{seam.key_b}} inches across at the base.

The picture shows where those joints sit in the frame.

:::box do "Worksheet 5: my cut list"
| | Long | Short |
|---|---|---|
| Chord (radius × factor, in) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Bite for my stick width (in) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Cut length (chord − bite, in) | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| How many | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Colour I will mark them | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |

**Saw setups I will make, in order:** [[blank]] · **Key profiles:** [[blank]]
:::

:::box why "Why"
Only two edge lengths exist because the dome is an icosahedron subdivided once:
every edge is either half an original edge or a line between two midpoints. The
cut lengths differ from the chords by the pinwheel's bite, which is set by how
wide the stick is -- a fatter log means a bigger bite and shorter members for the
same dome. The fold angle plus the gap the key fills always adds up to the
{{cut.sector}}-degree wedge the tree was split into, which is why two keys close
the whole dome.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Never cut a member to its chord: it will be too long by the bite, forty times
over. Keep the two lengths in separate, marked stacks. The short-sided panels
have a left and a right side that differ by about two inches over five feet --
pick them from their stacks in order, never by eye. And the volumes print more
than one cut list; the comparison page at the back says which is which.
:::

plan/panel.title: Plan the Jig and the Panel Run
plan/panel.deck: One bench, twelve stages, forty panels in two shapes
plan/panel.body:
**What you are deciding:** how the forty panels get made -- the bench, the jig, the
order, the marking, and how long it takes.

## The reference answer

One flat bench, set up twice: once for the {{dome.aaa}} equal-sided panels and
once for the {{dome.bab}} short-sided ones. The jig holds each member by its two
flat sawn faces against fixed stops, guides the saw for the butt cut and the
flush cut, and takes each panel through twelve stages from bare bench to finished
triangle. The picture is the jig the simulator models.

The forty-hour clock gives this part of the work two estimated lines:
{{clock.cut_h}} hours for cutting both ends and drilling, and {{clock.panels_h}}
hours for bolting members into panels on the jig. Both are **estimates** -- reasoned
from the owner's process, not yet timed on a full run -- and the clock's error
allowance exists partly because of them.

Plan for the learning curve. The first panel off a new jig is a rehearsal, the
second is nearly right, and the fourth is usually the first good one. The
practice panels are not waste: they become test pieces, and the spare struts in
the pile pay for them.

:::box do "Worksheet 6: my panel run"
| | My plan |
|---|---|
| Bench size and where it stands (flat, level, under cover) | [[blank]] |
| Setup 1: equal-sided panels, how many | [[blank]] |
| Setup 2: short-sided panels, how many | [[blank]] |
| Marking scheme (colour per length, side per stripe) | [[blank]] |
| Practice panels allowed for | [[blank]] |
| Panels per day I expect | [[blank]] |
| Days for the run | [[blank]] |
| Where finished panels are stacked, dry | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
Forty panels that agree with each other close into a dome; forty panels that are
each nearly right do not, because their small differences add up round the
rings. A jig makes agreement automatic: the position is measured once, when the
