stops are set, and never again.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
The bench must be flat -- a twist in the bench is a twist in every panel. Locate
every member from its sawn faces, never its bark. Check the first panel against
its drawing before you build the second. Pick one pinwheel direction and use it
for every panel.
:::

plan/raise.title: Choose How It Goes Up
plan/raise.deck: On blocks and props, or in the air between trees -- and who holds what
plan/raise.body:
**What you are deciding:** how forty panels become one standing frame, and who
holds what while it happens.

## Two reference answers

**On the ground, course by course.** The panels go up on level blocks, bottom
ring first: a first course of {{ring.first}} panels ({{ring.first_up}} standing
on the floor ring and {{ring.first_down}} inverted between them), then a second
of {{ring.second}}, then the {{ring.cap}} round the top. Each course leans on the
one below and on props from inside until the top closes; then the shell carries
itself. The clock estimates {{clock.raise_h}} hours for lifting the panels into a
shell.

**In the air, between living trees.** This is the owner's own plan, and Volume A
gives it a chapter. An X of wire rope is stretched between four trees about
{{web.square_m}} metres apart, tied about {{web.tie1_m}} metres up, with a spiral
over the footprint. A {{web.winch_lb}}-pound 12-volt winch lifts each triangle
flat in a three-leg harness; the triangles are joined in the air and the finished
dome is left hanging. The owner has **weighed** the real struts at
{{web.strut_lo}} to {{web.strut_hi}} kilograms each, so a triangle weighs
{{web.tri_lo}} to {{web.tri_hi}} kilograms -- and the winch is rated
{{web.winch_x}} times the heaviest one.

The numbers that argue against it are printed too. Today's winch lifts about
{{web.now_pct}} per cent of the whole dome, so a one-piece lift needs the
planned {{web.up_lo}} to {{web.up_hi}} times bigger winch. The whole frame weighs
{{web.frame_lo}} to {{web.frame_hi}} kilograms. And an unguyed tree's margin is
{{web.tree1}} at the design sag but only {{web.tree1_taut}} if the web is pulled
tighter -- below one, the tree fails -- so the trees are guyed back to others.

:::box do "Worksheet 7: how mine goes up"
| | My plan |
|---|---|
| Method: ground course-by-course, or air | [[blank]] |
| Crew on the day, by name | [[blank]] |
| Props: how many, how long, from what | [[blank]] |
| Lifting gear and its rating | [[blank]] |
| Anchor trees, guying, who rated them | [[blank]] |
| Weather window, and the day we stop | [[blank]] |
| Where nobody stands while anything is lifted | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
A dome is a mechanism until it closes and a structure afterwards: before the top
panels go in, each course needs to be held; after, every triangle holds every
other. Lifting finished panels instead of loose sticks is what makes one person's
raising possible at all.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Never stand under anything that is hanging -- a triangle, a dome, or the rope that
holds them. Rigging, anchor trees and winches carry real loads that no book can
rate; that is an engineer's job and an arborist's. Raise in calm weather only:
a half-closed dome is a sail.
:::

plan/skin.title: Choose the First Coat
plan/skin.deck: One watertight layer now, warm layers when the winters ask
plan/skin.body:
**What you are deciding:** the first coat -- what keeps the water out now -- and how
the building gets warmer over the years.

## The reference answer

**One watertight layer, and only one.** The standard article's skin is a
rain-slick cap over the whole shell -- the "shower cap" -- priced at
{{money.cap}} dollars. Everything else goes under it, where it stays dry.

**Warmth one winter at a time.** Under the cap go quilted layers sewn from
recycled clothing: about {{tt_quilt.shirts_per_layer}} t-shirts a layer, each
adding R-{{tt_quilt.r_per_layer}}, at {{tt_quilt.usd_per_layer}} dollars a layer
through the quilt network the project proposes. Three layers make
R-{{tt_quilt.stacked_r}}. The picture shows how the heating bill falls layer by
layer -- the first layer pays back fastest, and each one after buys a little less.

**A harder shell later, if ever.** The same dome with a laminated hull instead of
the cap lists at {{money.hard_price}} dollars. The cap is the standard; the hull
is the upgrade, and nothing about the frame changes between them.

**The wood's own finish.** Volume A chars and oils the outside bark faces and
keeps oil off the faces a seal or gasket must stick to. Its estimate for the
frame is {{lin.allow_gal}} gallons of linseed oil and {{lin.labour_h}} hours of
hand work.

:::box do "Worksheet 8: my first coat"
| | My plan |
|---|---|
| The one watertight layer | [[blank]] |
| How it is fastened down at the rim | [[blank]] |
| Quilt layers before the first winter | [[blank]] |
| Where moisture from inside goes | [[blank]] |
| Where water drains at the rim | [[blank]] |
| Finish on the wood, and where it is kept off | [[blank]] |
| Budget for the skin | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
Water is the silent killer of wooden buildings, and a shell with {{dome.seams}}
seams has {{dome.seams}} places to lose that fight. One continuous watertight
layer outside everything else means there is only one surface to keep perfect.
Inside, warm damp air condenses on anything colder than its dew point, so the
shell is planned to breathe and to drain at the rim rather than to be sealed.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Never seal the inside face airtight against the frame; give the water a path.
Keep oil off any surface a tape, sealant or gasket must stick to. And oily rags
can catch fire by themselves -- they go straight into a lidded metal tin of
water, outside, the same day.
:::

plan/ground.title: Choose the Ground
plan/ground.deck: Gravel, deck, piers, slab or a pad somebody else owns
plan/ground.body:
**What you are deciding:** what the dome stands on -- or hangs from -- and how the
ring is kept round, level and tied down.

## The reference answer

Volume A prices the grounds a dome can stand on. For the standard article: a
compacted gravel base, {{money.gravel}} dollars; a framed deck on piers,
{{money.deck}}; a full concrete slab, {{money.slab}}. Across the Dome Creator's
foundation menu the cabin's whole price swings by {{sty.by_foundation_span}}
dollars, from {{sty.by_foundation_lo_usd}} on {{sty.by_foundation_lo}} to
{{sty.by_foundation_hi_usd}} on a {{sty.by_foundation_hi}}. The picture lines
the options up.

The cheapest ground is ground somebody else already built. The project proposes
**pads**: serviced platforms a host builds once and rents, so the dome on top can
leave. On a pad, the platform -- {{money.pad}} dollars of it for the standard
article -- is the host's bill, not the dome owner's.

Two upgrades at the edge are worth planning from the start. A short straight
**pony wall** under the rim lifts the dome and turns the low ring into standing
room: on Volume B's {{tt_pony.floor}}-square-foot reference floor, a three-foot
wall costs {{tt_pony.cost_3}} dollars and buys back {{tt_pony.gain_3}} square feet,
taking the usable share from {{tt_pony.pct_0}} to {{tt_pony.pct_3}} per cent. And
a **brim** at the rim throws rain clear of the base and can catch it in a tank.

:::box do "Worksheet 9: my ground"
| | My plan |
|---|---|
| Ground: gravel, deck, piers, slab, pad, or hung | [[blank]] |
| Cost | [[blank]] |
| How the ring is set out (centre stake, string) | [[blank]] |
| The three ring checks: when, by whom | [[blank]] |
| How the ring is tied down against wind | [[blank]] |
| Drainage away from the ring | [[blank]] |
| Pony wall? Height | [[blank]] |
| Who checks the footing for my soil and frost | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
A dome puts its weight on a circle, not a floor, so the footing belongs under the
ring -- concrete across the middle carries no frame at all. The ring is the one
place error accumulates instead of being absorbed. And wind over a dome lifts it
like a wing, so the ring has to be tied down, not just set down.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Never skip the hold-downs. Footing depth, frost and soil bearing are site
questions for somebody who can read your ground. And if you hang the dome
instead, the trees and rigging are your foundation -- see chapter seven, and
treat them with the same seriousness.
:::

plan/uses.title: Choose What It Is For
plan/uses.deck: Fifteen buildings from one body, priced, and the utility buildings that pay for themselves
plan/uses.body:
**What you are deciding:** what the building is for -- which, on this frame, is a
decision about panels, not about structure.

## The reference answer

The project's product line starts from the **stem cell**: the bare frame, its
skin, the utility core in the middle and one blank panel. Everything a building
is *for* -- windows, doors, a skylight, a stove flue, benches, a sink, a rack of
shelves -- is a set of panels and modules added to that body. Volume A prices
{{seed.count}} named fit-outs on the same frame:

    {{seed.table}}

Look at how many of them are **utility buildings**: cold storage, a workshop, a
garage, a studio, a sauna, a growing room. For most families the first dome is
not the house. It is the building that makes the house work better -- the dry
workshop, the root cellar above ground, the greenhouse that grows food in March
-- and it earns its keep while the family learns the method on something that
does not have to be slept in.

Style is a separate decision. The Dome Creator dresses the same cabin twelve
ways; the dearest style costs {{sty.style_ratio}} times the cheapest, and the menus
that move the price most are, in order: {{sty.ranking}}.

:::box do "Worksheet 10: what mine is for"
| | My plan |
|---|---|
| First purpose | [[blank]] |
| Second purpose, five years on | [[blank]] |
| Panels it needs: windows, door, skylight, louvre, flue | [[blank]] |
| Modules it needs: water, drain, power, heat | [[blank]] |
| The fit-out above closest to mine, and its price | [[blank]] |
| Does it need a permit as a dwelling, or as an accessory building? | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
Because every panel is a separate framed triangle, the building's purpose lives
in its forty openings, not in its walls. A frame that has not decided what it is
can be re-decided later for the price of new panels -- which is what makes it a
stem cell rather than a shed. The core carries the services and is built to
unbolt and move to the next dome.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Anything with water needs a drain beside it. Power-hungry modules -- a sauna
heater above all -- change what the electrical panel and any battery bank have
to be. And the line between a shed and a dwelling is a legal one: ask your
building department which side your plan is on before you build it.
:::

plan/count.title: Your Clock and Your Budget
plan/count.deck: The forty-hour clock, the whole build's hours, and the invoice line by line
plan/count.body:
**What you are deciding:** how many hours and how many dollars -- and which of
those numbers are real yet.

## The reference answer: hours

The title's forty hours are the frame, from wedges to standing, counted stage by
stage in Volume A:

    {{clock.table}}

Felling, the skin, the floor, doors and windows are not on that clock. The whole
build is about {{money.labour_hours}} hours of labour. The paperback counts its
forty hours differently -- erection alone, with splitting added on top -- and the
comparison page at the back of this book sets the two clocks side by side.

## The reference answer: dollars

The standard article -- the stem-cell dome as a product, built by somebody else
at a wage and sold with a stated margin -- is invoiced line by line:

    {{kick.w_invoice}}

It costs {{money.cost}} dollars to make, carries a markup of {{money.profit}}
dollars, and lists at {{money.price}} dollars: {{money.per_sqft}} dollars a square
foot of floor, on ground priced separately. The frame -- the part this method is
about -- is the smallest line: {{money.frame}} dollars. Building it yourself
removes the labour line and the markup; it does not remove the cap, the core or
the panels.

:::box do "Worksheet 11: my clock and my budget"
| Stage | My hours | Measured or estimated? | My dollars |
|---|---|---|---|
| Felling and bucking | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Splitting | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Cutting, panels, raising | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| The skin | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| The ground | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| The core and the panels | [[blank]] | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Allowance for getting it wrong | [[blank]] | declared | [[blank]] |
| **Total** | [[blank]] | | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
A plan that does not say which of its numbers are measured is a plan nobody can
check, including you. And money you avoid spending is real but it is not income:
it only counts if you were going to buy the thing anyway. The volumes keep that
distinction on every page.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Prices go stale; check every one locally before you rely on it. Log your real
hours and real receipts as you go -- the next family's plan starts from them.
Do not leave the allowance out because the work feels easy on paper.
:::

plan/care.title: Your Safety Plan
plan/care.deck: Who signs off, who holds the saw, who stands where, and what is never done alone
plan/care.body:
**What you are deciding:** who signs off, who does which job, what everybody
wears, and what is never done alone. This worksheet is the one that gets signed.

## The reference answer

Both volumes open the same way: *this book is not engineering.* It prices loads
and does not rate them. Snow, wind, the ground under the ring, the rigging that
lifts a dome and the trees it hangs from are a licensed engineer's numbers; the
permit, the setbacks and whether a building may be slept in are the building
department's; electrical and plumbing connections are licensed trades'. The plan
reaches all three before the first tree is cut.

At the log: a helmet with a mesh visor, ear protection, gloves, boots and
chainsaw chaps on every cut, and a second person present for every session.
Felling uses a planned notch, a hinge left whole, a cleared escape route, and
everyone else at least two tree-lengths away -- the picture shows why the hinge is
the whole art. On the ladder and at the lift: three points of contact, a spotter,
and nobody, ever, under a hanging load. Any lift heavier than
{{en.two_person_kg}} kilograms is a two-person lift.

:::box do "Worksheet 12: our safety plan"
| | Name / answer | Signed |
|---|---|---|
| Engineer who reviewed the design | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Building department contact and permit | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Electrician and plumber | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Who is trained on the saw | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| The second person at every saw session | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Our stop word | [[blank]] | everyone |
| First-aid kit and who knows how to use it | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
| Address to give an ambulance | [[blank]] | |
| Where children are while the saw runs | [[blank]] | [[blank]] |
:::

:::box why "Why"
The method's honesty about what it does not know is what makes it safe to try:
every place a figure becomes a load, the book stops and names who decides. A plan
that has those names on it is a plan you can stand behind.
:::

:::box watch "Watch out"
Fatigue causes more accidents than ignorance; the clock's allowance for getting
it wrong is also a rest allowance -- use it. Stop the work in wind, in rain on
ladders, and whenever anybody calls the stop word.
:::

build/tree.title: Fell and Buck
build/tree.deck: Put the trees on the ground and cut them to the one length
build/tree.body:
The trees come down: felled with a planned notch and hinge, limbed, and bucked
into sections of one length, cutting out the bends and the flare. This is the
most dangerous work in the whole build, and the books do not soften it.

:::box do "Before you start"
Your safety plan from rung three is signed. The fall line of every tree is
chosen from its lean, the wind and the landing ground, and an escape route is
cleared for each. The second person knows their job is to watch the crown and
stay out of the fall. Your section length is decided and cut into a story pole.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Every section is cut, counted twice, stacked off the ground, and the count
matches the struts your plan needs plus spares.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Read the felling and limbing procedures in Volume B against your own training. Is
every instruction about the notch, the hinge, the back cut and a log under tension
correct for the cases a first-time feller will meet?
:::

build/split.title: Rip the Wedges
build/split.deck: The saw, the three passes and the stacked pile
build/split.body:
The sections become wedges: each one cradled, ripped through the pith three
times over with the chainsaw, and the eight wedges stacked bark-up on spacers to
dry. This is the measured part of the clock, so time yourself and keep the log.

:::box do "Before you start"
A ripping chain, filed; bar oil and mixed fuel; a cradle that stops the round
from rolling; spacer sticks and a dry place for the stack. The saw's setup and
safety page in Volume B has been read by everybody who will be at the log.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
The pile holds every member the frame needs plus spares, graded in four passes --
bend, knot, bearing end, pith -- and your own rate, in wedges per session, is
written down.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is the claim that a small consumer saw can rip six-foot green sections, at the
measured rate, believable to someone who runs saws for a living?
:::

build/triangle.title: Trust the Frame
build/triangle.deck: Why the frame forgives a rough stick, from the forces up
build/triangle.body:
Before the frame goes up, understand why it will stand: why a rough wedge is a
good strut, what it gives up as a beam, and where the frame forgives and where it
does not. These chapters are the argument the whole method rests on.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung two's wobble test, built and pushed. Rung three's worksheet on where your
care goes, filled in.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
You can explain to somebody else why the wedge loses to a two-by-four as a beam
and wins as a strut, and why that is the right comparison for a dome.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Volume B compares the wedge with a two-by-four on area, stiffness and bending
strength, and prints the column the wedge loses. Is the comparison fair, and is
its conclusion -- that a dome loads its members mostly along their length --
stated with the right caution?
:::

build/dome.title: Solve Your Dome
build/dome.deck: Size it from the dome you want or the tree you have, and check it both ways
build/dome.body:
Size the dome for real: from the dome you want, from the tree you have, or both
-- then run the round trip that proves the two calculations agree before
anything is cut.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung three's worksheets one and four, filled in, with the convention -- chord or
cut member -- written at the top.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Your radius, your longest member and your tree count agree in both directions,
and you know which of the books' two domes yours is closer to.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The two volumes size their domes from "six feet" in two different ways and get
two different domes. Read the comparison page at the back of this book. Is the
difference explained clearly enough that a builder could not mix the two up?
:::

build/joint.title: Cut the Joints
build/joint.deck: The pinwheel, the butt cut, the long head and the key
build/joint.body:
Cut the joints: the one compound cut at the butt, the head left deliberately long,
the flush cut that makes the panel true, and the key in every seam. This is where
the tolerance of the whole method lives.

:::box do "Before you start"
The cut list from rung three, worksheet five. A saw setup for each distinct butt
cut, proved on one offcut before the class is cut. Key stock for both profiles.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Every member is cut to its class, marked, and stacked by class, and a test butt
cut sits flat on its neighbour's face with no rocking.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The volumes describe the butt cut, the head overfit and the keys in several
places. Do they agree with each other -- on the overfit allowance, on whether
the build uses one key profile or two, and on when the keys go in?
:::

build/panel.title: Run the Jig
build/panel.deck: One flat board, forty identical panels
build/panel.body:
Build the jig, then run it: forty panels in two shapes, each located against the
same stops, screwed, flush-cut, checked against its drawing and stacked.

:::box do "Before you start"
A flat bench, set up for the first shape. The marking scheme decided. The panel
drawings printed for checking. Spares counted for the practice panels.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Forty panels are stacked by shape, each one checked against its drawing, and
the jig's practice panels are kept as test pieces.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The jig chapters say "one bench, forty panels" while the dome has two panel
shapes. Is it clear how one bench builds both, and how the short-sided panels'
left and right sides are kept from being swapped?
:::

build/raise.title: Raise It
build/raise.deck: Bottom ring first, props until the top closes
build/raise.body:
Raise it: the bottom ring set and checked, each course keyed and screwed as it
goes, props under every leaning panel until the top closes, and then the props
out.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung three's worksheet seven: the method chosen, the crew named, the props cut,
the weather watched, and the place nobody stands while anything is lifted.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
The frame stands closed with no props, and the ring measures round across every
opposite pair of corners.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
If the dome is to be hung from trees, the rigging, the trees and the winch carry
real loads. Do the volumes say clearly enough that those loads are an engineer's
and an arborist's to rate, and that nobody stands under a hanging load?
:::

build/skin.title: Close the Shell
build/skin.deck: One watertight layer, the seams, the water, the finish
build/skin.body:
Close the shell: one watertight layer over everything, every seam lapped so water
runs downhill over it, the rim drained, the inside allowed to breathe, and the
wood finished where a finish belongs.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung three's worksheet eight. The rag station set up before any oil is opened. A
dry spell long enough to get the watertight layer on.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
A night of hard rain leaves the inside dry, and you know where the water from
the inside goes.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The books say the skin is the part that must be right. Is the advice on sheet
goods, seams and condensation specific enough to be followed, and does it agree
between the two volumes -- for instance, on which faces of the wood are oiled?
:::

build/ground.title: Set the Ground
build/ground.deck: The floor, the ring and what it all stands on
build/ground.body:
Set the ground: the circle staked from a fixed centre, the ten points set level,
the footing under the ring rather than the middle, the hold-downs in, and the
floor built to stand on.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung three's worksheet nine. Your footing reviewed by somebody who knows your soil
and frost depth.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
The five diameters across the ring agree, the ten points share one level, and
every base point is tied down.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The volumes describe the build's frame as standing on blocks, on a ring, and
hanging from trees, in different places. Is it clear which is the reference
build and which are options?
:::

build/uses.title: Make It Livable
build/uses.deck: Doors, windows, services and a round room to live in
build/uses.body:
Make it livable: the openings cut without breaking the triangles, the round room
furnished the way its headroom wants, and the services -- power, water, heat --
run through the column and the seams.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung three's worksheet ten. The electrician and plumber on your safety plan
booked for their parts.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Somebody can sleep, cook or work in it -- whatever it is for -- warm, dry and
legally.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
A doorway at the rim of a dome is a triangle. Do the volumes say clearly how
tall it is and how a full-height door is made, whether by a riser wall or
another way?
:::

build/count.title: Log Every Hour
build/count.deck: What the build cost in money, hours and the body
build/count.body:
Log every hour and every receipt while you build -- not afterwards. The books'
own counts are partly estimates; a real build's log is the measurement that
turns them into facts.

:::box do "Before you start"
A notebook at the work, and the stages from rung three's worksheet eleven written
at the top of its pages.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Your build has a log with every stage's hours and every receipt, each one
labelled measured.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The two volumes count their forty hours differently, and both report whole-build
hours elsewhere. Read the comparison page and the hours chapters together. Could
a reader come away with the wrong idea of how long the whole build takes?
:::

build/care.title: The Rules at the Log
build/care.deck: Chainsaw, felling, ladders, lifts and trades
build/care.body:
The rules at the log, on the ladder and at the lift -- gathered from both volumes
into one reading. Read these before the saw starts, and read them again on the
morning of every felling day.

:::box do "Before you start"
Rung three's worksheet twelve, signed by everybody who will be on site.
:::

:::box done "Done when"
Every person on site has read these chapters and can say the stop word and the
never-alone rule.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is there any instruction anywhere in either volume that you would not want a
first-time builder to follow exactly as written? Mark it.
:::

design/tree.title: Other Trees, Other Sticks
design/tree.deck: What changes with the species, the trunk and the market
design/tree.body:
The method was never pine's; it was the sector's. Other species split, dry and
last differently, an oval trunk splits by area rather than by angle, and a tree's
value depends entirely on what you ask it to be.

:::box do "Design exercise"
List the species that grow within a short drive of you. For each, find whether it
splits straight, whether it resists rot in the ground, and how fast it dries. Pick
the one you would build from, and say why.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is the advice on other species cautious enough about rot-prone wood near the
ground and about spiral grain?
:::

design/split.title: Other Sections
design/split.deck: When your sticks are rectangles, tubes or bought
design/split.body:
The solid split wedge is the reference member, not the only one. Rectangular
sticks, bought lumber and the whole catalogue of frame materials and sections are
priced on the same dome, so you can see exactly what the wedge buys and what it
gives up.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Price the reference frame twice: once in split wedges from your own trees, once
in bought rectangular lumber. What does the difference pay for, and what does it
cost you in hours?
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Do the books keep the wedge's real advantage -- wood kept from your own trees --
separate from its disadvantages as a beam, every time they compare it?
:::

design/triangle.title: Hubs or No Hubs
design/triangle.deck: The trade this method answers, and when the other side wins
design/triangle.body:
Every dome builder chooses between hubs and no hubs. A hub makes every corner the
same factory part and needs identical struts; the pinwheel needs no connector and
costs extra wood. Both are good systems for different builders.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Decide which system suits you, from three questions: who cuts the wood, who
assembles it, and whether the dome will ever be taken apart. Write your three
answers and your choice.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is the extra wood the hubless frame uses -- every panel owning all three of its
members -- stated plainly wherever the method's savings are claimed?
:::

design/dome.title: Other Shapes and Sizes
design/dome.deck: Frequencies, zomes, hexagons and the 3V panel dome
design/dome.body:
Change the shape: a different size, a higher frequency with more and shorter
members, a zome whose panels are flat by construction, a hexagon dome with one
strut length, or the popular three-frequency panel dome most bought plans build.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Choose the floor you need. Find the smallest shape in these chapters that gives it
with sticks one person can still carry. Write down its panel count and its
longest stick.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Check one geometric claim in these chapters yourself -- the count of pentagons, the
two lengths, the zome's flat panels -- and mark whether it holds.
:::

design/joint.title: The Seam as a Service Channel
design/joint.deck: Water and wire in the gap the key leaves
design/joint.body:
The gap a key leaves between two members is a channel that runs through every
seam of the dome, and it can carry water lines, wire and sensor cable -- though
not a round air duct without growing the dome.

:::box do "Design exercise"
List the services your building needs. Which ones fit in the channel, and which
need the central column? Mark where the one place not to drill is.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is it clear which services the channel is meant for, and that no pressure fitting
is ever buried in a seam?
:::

design/panel.title: Panels With a Purpose
design/panel.deck: Doors, windows and panels that do a job
design/panel.body:
Panels decide what the building does. A doorway is a whole panel left out and
framed; a window replaces part of a panel and re-triangulates around the glass; a
panel can be a skylight, a louvre, a flue or a shelf.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Take your plan from rung three. Mark which of the forty triangles are windows,
which is the door, which is the flue and which stay blank. Count the special
panels.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Does every opening the books propose keep every load path triangulated?
:::

design/raise.title: Hang It
design/raise.deck: The owner's way: build it in the air between living trees
design/raise.body:
The owner's way of building is in the air: a web of wire rope between living
trees, a battery winch, each triangle lifted flat and joined in place, and the
finished dome left hanging where the trees hold it.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Walk your land and find four trees that could form a square of about the size
the volumes use. Measure their trunks and note their species and health. Would you
trust them -- and who would you ask?
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The sky web is the owner's plan, partly tested. Are its measured parts -- the
weighed struts, the winch -- kept clearly apart from its modelled parts and its
open questions?
:::

design/skin.title: Style It
design/skin.deck: Twelve styles, every skin, every cladding, priced
design/skin.body:
Style it: the same frame dressed every way the Dome Creator can dress it --
twelve styles rendered, every panel material on every frame material, every
cladding on every ground -- each one a priced rebuild of the same dome.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Pick the style closest to what you want. Then change one menu at a time -- the
panel, the cladding, the ground -- and write down how the price moves. Which menu
matters most for your design?
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The price tables are rebuilt by software. Pick any three prices and check whether
the materials they assume are realistic where you live.
:::

design/ground.title: Pads and Platforms
design/ground.deck: Ground you build once and lend to the next dome
design/ground.body:
Ground you build once and lend to the next dome: the pad, what it costs, what a
host earns from it, and the pony wall and brim that fix what a bare dome gets
wrong at its edge.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Price your ground two ways: as a pad you own, and as a pad you rent. Over ten
years, which is cheaper for you, and what would change your mind?
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The pad's payback depends on how often it is rented, which no model can know. Is
that assumption stated wherever a payback is quoted?
:::

design/uses.title: Fifteen Buildings From One Body
design/uses.deck: The stem cell, its core and its catalogue
design/uses.body:
The stem cell's whole catalogue: the undifferentiated body, the utility core
that outlives it, fifteen buildings from one frame, and the Dome Creator's twelve
finished designs -- the place to find the building that is yours.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Choose one utility building -- storage, a workshop, a greenhouse, a studio -- and
one home. Price both from the catalogue. Which would you build first, and why?
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is it clear which fit-outs are priced from real quotes and which from declared
estimates?
:::

design/count.title: Price It Item by Item
design/count.deck: Every line, every item, every package
design/count.body:
Price it item by item: every equipment item, every package, every part with its
minutes to fit, the standard article's invoice, and where a house's money goes
whatever shape it is.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Build the price of your own design line by line from these tables, and mark every
line measured, estimated or declared. Then add the hours.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The volumes quote several prices for "the frame" and "the building", from
different models and sizes. Is it clear which one applies to which question?
:::

design/care.title: Design It Safe
design/care.deck: What a design must hand to an engineer, and how
design/care.body:
Designing safe is mostly knowing what to hand to whom: what an engineer needs to
see, what the building department needs to read, and how to build so that a
part can be changed later without weakening the rest.

:::box do "Design exercise"
Write the one page you would send an engineer about your design: its size, its
frame, its skin, its ground, its loads, and the questions you need answered.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
If you are an engineer: what would you need to see that the books do not yet
provide?
:::

experiment/tree.title: Weigh Your Own Wood
experiment/tree.deck: What a tree is worth, measured on your own trees
experiment/tree.body:
**The open question:** what is a tree on *your* land actually worth to *you*, on
each rung of the value ladder -- standing, as firewood, sawn, split, as a
building?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Pick one tree you could fell. Measure it as on rung two. Weigh one green section
(a bathroom scale and some arithmetic will do), split it, and weigh the wedges as
they dry over a month. Price the same volume as firewood and as lumber at your
local yard. Write down every number with its source.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The value ladder multiplies a tree's stump price many times over. Is it clear on
every rung that a substitution value is not income?
:::

experiment/split.title: Time Your Own Split
experiment/split.deck: Your rate at the log, and what an hour there buys
experiment/split.body:
**The open question:** is the measured splitting rate typical -- and what is an
hour at the log really worth against an hour's wage?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Time ten full splitting sessions, with the same saw and the same chain filing
routine, and log the wedges from each, the fuel used and how you felt at the end.
Plot your rate against session number. Then compute your own rate's value against
bought lumber, exactly as the hour chapter does.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is the measured rate described with enough detail -- saw, chain, log size, session
length -- for somebody else to repeat it?
:::

experiment/triangle.title: What the Ugly One Taught
experiment/triangle.deck: The frame that should not have stood, and why it did
experiment/triangle.body:
**The open question:** how rough can the frame be before it stops forgiving? The
Frankendome -- built from mismatched salvage with no two members alike -- stood
for months, and it is the project's evidence and its warning at once.

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Under an engineer's guidance, build two test panels: one from your best-graded
wedges and one from wedges you would normally reject. Load each the same way, the
same small amount, and measure how much it moves. Never load anything to failure
near a person, and never test a panel anyone will build into a home.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Do the stories of the earlier domes draw the right lesson -- that triangles forgive,
but that forgiveness is not a structural rating?
:::

experiment/dome.title: Check the Geometry Yourself
experiment/dome.deck: Derive the two lengths four ways and close the round trip
experiment/dome.body:
**The open question:** can you derive every number in the dome yourself, and does
it agree with the software that printed it?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
From the twelve corners of an icosahedron, derive the two chord factors by hand --
the volumes show four independent routes. Then take the paper dome from rung two,
measure its edges, and compute the radius they imply. How close is the paper to
the arithmetic? For the brave: run the project's own software and compare.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Mathematicians and engineers: check one derivation in these chapters end to end,
and mark any step that is asserted rather than shown.
:::

experiment/joint.title: Run the Seam Climate
experiment/joint.deck: Dew points, levels, drawers and plates -- the experiment in the gap
experiment/joint.body:
**The open question:** can the seams of a dome manage its own moisture -- sorting
air by dew point, draining at the rim, keeping wood dry -- with a small controller,
a fan, desiccant drawers and cold plates?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Fit two cheap temperature-and-humidity loggers: one in a seam channel, one in the
room. Log through a season. Compute the dew point of each from its readings, and
mark every day the seam's surface fell below the room's dew point. That is the
condition the whole seam-climate system exists to prevent.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The seam-climate chapters are modelled, not measured. Are their caveats -- what has
not been built -- as prominent as their arithmetic?
:::

experiment/panel.title: Count Every Piece
experiment/panel.deck: The software that numbers every piece and draws every picture
experiment/panel.body:
**The open question:** how far can software carry a hand-built method -- numbering
every piece, drawing every cut, rendering every picture -- and where must a person
still decide?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Number every member of your build as the every-piece chapter does, mark the
numbers on the wood, and record where each one ended up in the frame. Afterwards,
compare the software's plan with what actually happened, and list every place they
differed and why.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Is it clear to a non-programmer what the software does, what it needs, and that a
build does not require running it?
:::

experiment/raise.title: The Sky Web
experiment/raise.deck: The winch, the web and the owner's weighed struts
experiment/raise.body:
**The open question:** can a whole dome be built and lived in up in the trees --
the web, the winch, the lashings, the skin -- and what do living trees do under
that load over years?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
With an arborist and an engineer: instrument the anchor trees of a sky web with
simple tilt gauges, log their movement through wind and seasons, and weigh every
strut as it goes up. Record every lift's time. Publish the log, including the
lifts that went wrong.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Arborists especially: what do the sky-web chapters not yet consider about the
anchor trees' health, roots and long-term response?
:::

experiment/skin.title: Log a Winter
experiment/skin.deck: The measurement this whole project is waiting for
experiment/skin.body:
**The open question -- the most important one in this book:** what does a skinned
dome actually do through a winter? How warm, how dry, how much heat does it take,
and does the moisture plan work?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Log a winter. Temperature and humidity outside, in the room, and at every layer of
the skin; the heat put in each day; every quilt layer added and when. Note every
morning of condensation and where it was. The project's own costed plan names this
exact measurement as its first priority, and promises to publish it whichever way
it comes out.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Every energy figure in both volumes is modelled. Is that said everywhere an energy
figure is quoted?
:::

experiment/ground.title: The Pad Network
experiment/ground.deck: Hosts, tenants, resale -- proposed, priced, not yet built
experiment/ground.body:
**The open question:** could a network of serviced pads let a family own a building
without owning land -- and would a used dome hold its value when it moves?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Survey your area: who has a level, serviced piece of ground they would rent to a
dome? What would they charge? What would your local building department say about
a movable dwelling on it? Write down what you find and where the books' assumptions
were right or wrong.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
The network is the least-built idea in the project. Is it presented as a proposal
everywhere it appears?
:::

experiment/uses.title: Who It Is For
experiment/uses.deck: A home people can afford to start with -- and why this author cares
experiment/uses.body:
**The open question:** who is this for, really -- and what would a small home you
owned, could improve as you went, and could take with you have meant to somebody
starting out? The author's own answer, and Buckminster Fuller's, are in these
chapters.

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Ask three people who might need a building like this -- a young family, a single
parent, somebody starting a business -- what they would use one for first, and
what would stop them. Write down their words, not yours. Compare them with the
catalogue.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Does the book make its case for who it is for without over-promising what a dome
can do for a family?
:::

experiment/count.title: Publish Your Numbers
experiment/count.deck: Real hours, real receipts, and the corrections
experiment/count.body:
**The open question:** what does a real build cost, start to finish, in hours and in
money -- measured, not estimated -- and where were the books wrong?

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Publish your build's log: every stage's hours, every receipt, every rejected wedge,
every rain day. Then write the chapter the paperback ends with -- what you would do
differently -- and send it to the author. The next edition is built from logs like
yours.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
Find one number in either volume you think is wrong and say why. Corrections are
printed in this project, not hidden.
:::

experiment/care.title: Report the Near Misses
experiment/care.deck: Testing safely, and writing down what nearly went wrong
experiment/care.body:
**The open question:** what nearly went wrong? Safety improves fastest when the near
misses are written down, not just the accidents.

:::box do "An experiment you can run"
Keep a near-miss log for your whole build: date, what happened, what nearly
happened, why, and what you changed. Share it with the author and with the next
family. Every rule in rung four's safety card was once somebody's near miss.
:::

:::box check "For checkers"
What is the most dangerous moment in the whole method, in your judgement -- and
does the book treat it as the most dangerous?
:::
